en: Nāradasmṛti 1. Mātṛkā 1.
Judicial Procedure (Vyavahāra)
When men were single-mindedly devoted to Dharma and speakers of truth,
then there was no legal dispute, nor hatred, nor even envy.
When men were single-mindedly devoted to Dharma and speakers of truth, then there was no legal dispute, nor hatred, nor even envy.

When Dharma has perished among men, legal procedure (vyavahāra) comes into operation; and the king is appointed as the observer of legal procedures and the wielder of the rod of punishment. When Dharma has perished among men, legal procedure comes into operation; and the king is appointed as the observer of legal procedures and the wielder of the rod of punishment.
In this matter, two methods are proclaimed for the purpose of clarifying a disputed point between two litigants: written documents and witnesses. (Narada Smṛti 1.3)
It should be understood as having two characteristics: with superior and without superior.

That which is "with superior" is that in which there is a wager preceded by a written contract (*vilekhā*). It should be understood as having two characteristics: with superior and without superior. That which is "with superior" is that in which there is a wager preceded by a written contract.
In a dispute involving a wager, whichever of the two parties is defeated therein shall be made to pay the wager he himself made,
as well as the fine for defeat.
The essence of legal proceedings is declared to be the plaint;
if that is lost, the plaintiff fails, while he who crosses over it becomes the defendant.
The essence of legal proceedings is declared to be the plaint; if that is lost, the plaintiff fails, while he who crosses over it becomes the defendant.
Families, guilds, assemblies, and the appointed king are the foundations of legal proceedings; each subsequent one is more authoritative than the preceding.
He is proclaimed as having four feet, four stations, and four means; he is the one who brings fourfold benefit, who pervades the four,
and who performs the fourfold action.
It has eight limbs, eighteen titles, and likewise a hundred branches;
it has three origins, two types of legal proceedings, two doors,
and likewise two destinies.

Dharma, judicial procedure, custom, and royal edict— this four-legged judicial process consists of these, each subsequent one superseding the preceding. Dharma, judicial procedure, custom, and royal edict— this four-legged judicial process consists of these, each subsequent one superseding the preceding.
In that regard, Dharma is established in truth; legal procedure (vyavahāra), however, rests upon witnesses;
customary practice (caritra) resides in written records; and a royal edict (śāsana) lies in the king’s command.

(NarS 1.11) In that regard, Dharma is established in truth; legal procedure (vyavahāra), however, rests upon witnesses; customary practice (caritra) resides in written records; and a royal edict (śāsana) lies in the king’s command. (NarS 1.11)
Because he is accomplished through the means beginning with conciliation (*sāma*), he is called the "One of Four Means" (*catuḥsādhana*);

and because he protects the four stages of life (*āśrama*), he is the "One Beneficial to the Four" (*caturhita*). Because he is accomplished through the means beginning with conciliation, he is called the "One of Four Means"; and because he protects the four stages of life, he is the "One Beneficial to the Four."
Because it pervades the doers, the witnesses, the members of the court, and the king itself, part by part, it is therefore remembered as "pervading the four" (caturvyāpin).
Because he accomplishes these four—
dharma, artha, fame, and likewise public esteem— he is proclaimed as the "Accomplisher of the Four."
The king, his officials, the members of the court, the legal treatise, the calculator, the scribe, gold, fire, and water— this is declared to be the eightfold constituent of the court.

(Narada Smṛti 1.15) The king, his officials, the members of the court, the legal treatise, the calculator, the scribe, gold, fire, and water— this is declared to be the eightfold constituent of the court.
Recovery of debts, deposits, partnerships,
resumption of what has been given, and failure to perform agreed-upon service;
recovery of debts, deposits, partnerships, resumption of what has been given, and failure to perform agreed-upon service.
Non-payment of wages, as well as sale by one who is not the owner, non-delivery after having sold, and likewise rescission after having purchased.
The non-performance of agreements, disputes, and likewise those born of the field;
the union of man and woman, the partition of inheritance,
and then violence.
Likewise, verbal abuse, physical assault,
gambling, and miscellaneous offenses are declared; thus,
the legal system is remembered as having eighteen titles.

Another division of these very [paths] is recorded as one hundred and eight; due to the differences in the actions of human beings, it is said to have a hundred branches. (NarS 1.20) Another division of these very [paths] is recorded as one hundred and eight; due to the differences in the actions of human beings, it is said to have a hundred branches. (NarS 1.20)
Since it proceeds from these three—desire, anger, and greed—it is proclaimed as having three origins;
therefore, this triad is the cause of dispute.
Since it proceeds from these three—desire, anger, and greed—it is proclaimed as having three origins; therefore, this triad is the cause of dispute.
A lawsuit should be understood as being of two kinds:
based on suspicion and based on actual fact. Suspicion arises from association with the wicked, while actual fact is established by the discovery of stolen goods and the like.
Because it is connected with two sides, it is declared to have two doors:
of these two, the first statement is the *pakṣa* (the position), and the reply is the *pratipakṣa* (the counter-position).
Because it is connected with two sides, it is declared to have two doors: of these two, the first statement is the *pakṣa* (the position), and the reply is the *pratipakṣa* (the counter-position).
Because it follows both the real and the deceptive, it is said to have two courses:

the real is that which is connected with the true meaning, while the deceptive is that which is stated through error. Because it follows both the real and the deceptive, it is said to have two courses: the real is that which is connected with the true meaning, while the deceptive is that which is stated through error.
In that regard, a king who seeks to accomplish righteousness should tolerate the remaining forms of quibble;
he should resort only to what is factual, for prosperity has its root in righteousness.
For a self-disciplined king who adjudicates legal cases according to dharma,
seven virtues arise, just as seven flames arise from a fire. For a self-disciplined king who adjudicates legal cases according to dharma, seven virtues arise, just as seven flames arise from a fire.
Dharma, wealth, fame, the ripening of the world, the winning over of others, great honor from the subjects, and an eternal station in heaven.
Dharma, wealth, fame, the ripening of the world, the winning over of others, great honor from the subjects, and an eternal station in heaven.

Therefore, having ascended the seat of dharma, the king, free from envy, should be impartial toward all beings, upholding the vow of Vaivasvata. Therefore, having ascended the seat of dharma, the king, free from envy, should be impartial toward all beings, upholding the vow of Vaivasvata.
Placing the Dharmaśāstra before him and abiding by the opinion of the judge, he should,
with a concentrated mind,
examine the legal cases in their proper order.
The tradition (āgama) should be established first, then the subject matter of the legal proceeding (vyavahārapada), followed by the desire to know (vivitsā), and finally the decision (nirṇaya); thus,
the judicial process (darśana) is fourfold.

Without contradicting the treatises on Dharma and the treatises on worldly affairs (Artha), he should skillfully lead the course of legal proceedings by examining them closely according to the proper path.

Just as a hunter might track the path of a wounded deer by a trace of blood on its flanks, so too should one track the path of Dharma. Just as a hunter might track the path of a wounded deer by a trace of blood on its flanks, so too should one track the path of Dharma.

Where there may be a conflict between the Dharmaśāstra and the Arthaśāstra, one should set aside what is stated in the Arthaśāstra and practice what is stated in the Dharmaśāstra. Where there may be a conflict between the Dharmaśāstra and the Arthaśāstra, one should set aside what is stated in the Arthaśāstra and practice what is stated in the Dharmaśāstra.
But when there is a conflict with the Dharmaśāstras, even a legal proceeding that is logically sound is weaker than Dharma; for by such a proceeding,
Dharma is thereby subverted.
For the Blessed Dharma is subtle, beyond the senses, and difficult to investigate; therefore,
one should lead the course of legal procedure by means of direct perception.
Even one who is not a thief incurs the status of a thief, and a thief attains the status of a non-thief;
through legal procedure, Māṇḍavya—who was not a thief—was treated as a thief, while a thief attained the status of a non-thief.
Even one who is not a thief incurs the status of a thief, and a thief attains the status of a non-thief; through legal procedure, Māṇḍavya—who was not a thief—was treated as a thief.
A legal transaction entered into with women, at night, outside the village, within the house, or with enemies—
even if already concluded—
must be performed again.
Because of the profundity of legal disputes and because of the incapacity of even memory, one may,
out of a desire to know the truth, allow time to pass at will regarding debts and other such matters.
In cases of theft of cattle, land, gold, or women;
in cases of verbal or physical assault;
in urgent matters; in acts of violence; and in cases of false accusation, one should initiate legal proceedings immediately.
But he who proceeds with regard to a doubtful matter without having informed the king shall be punished by force, and his purpose shall not be accomplished.
The plaintiff shall restrain one who does not abide by the matter to be stated or who departs from those words, until the appearance for the summons.

Restriction may be of four kinds: restriction of place, restriction by time, restriction from travel, and likewise restriction from activity. One must not violate such a restriction while it remains unlifted.
In cases such as crossing a river, traversing a wilderness, or encountering a difficult region or calamity,
one who has not yet accomplished his purpose incurs no offense by bypassing that prohibition.

If one violates a prohibition that has been established during the period of prohibition, he shall be disciplined; otherwise, the one who imposed the prohibition shall become liable for punishment. (NarS 1.44) If one violates a prohibition that has been established during the period of prohibition, he shall be disciplined; otherwise, the one who imposed the prohibition shall become liable for punishment. (NarS 1.44)
One who desires to settle a marriage, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to perform a sacrifice, one situated in calamity, one attacked by another, and likewise one engaged in royal business.
Cowherds [should go] when the cattle are grazing; farmers when the crops are ripening;
artisans at their respective times; and soldiers during battle.
Cowherds [should go] when the cattle are grazing; farmers when the crops are ripening; artisans at their respective times; and soldiers during battle.
A minor (one who has not attained legal capacity), a messenger, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow,
and one in a precarious situation should not be detained;
nor should the king summon them.
One who has been charged should not bring a counter-charge against that person without first resolving the matter through other means;
nor should one who has been charged by another, or pierced [by an arrow], be fit to pierce [in return].

One who has been charged should not bring a counter-charge against that person without first resolving the matter through other means; nor should one who has been charged by another, or pierced [by an arrow], be fit to pierce [in return].
Whatever matter one may bring forward as a charge, one should not alter it;

nor should one shift to another position, for by doing so, one fails in respect to the former. Whatever matter one may bring forward as a charge, one should not alter it; nor should one shift to another position, for by doing so, one fails in respect to the former.
One should not bring a false accusation; for there is fault in one who brings a false accusation.
Whatever punishment is prescribed in that case shall fall upon the accuser.
One should not bring a false accusation; for there is fault in one who brings a false accusation. Whatever punishment is prescribed in that case shall fall upon the accuser.

Passing the time under some pretext, remaining silent even in an assembly, speaking words and then contradicting them— these are the characteristics of one who is losing ground. Passing the time under some pretext, remaining silent even in an assembly, speaking words and then contradicting them— these are the characteristics of one who is losing ground.

He who flees when summoned, or who, having arrived, does not engage in the dispute, shall be punished by the king and indeed defeated in that legal proceeding. He who flees when summoned, or who, having arrived, does not engage in the dispute, shall be punished by the king and indeed defeated in that legal proceeding.

In cases where a lawsuit has already been decided, evidence— whether documentary or testimonial— is rendered fruitless if it was not previously presented. In cases where a lawsuit has already been decided, evidence— whether documentary or testimonial— is rendered fruitless if it was not previously presented.

Just as the qualities of the rainy season are fruitless when the grains have already ripened, so too is the authority of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) fruitless for those whose legal proceedings have been settled. Just as the qualities of the rainy season are fruitless when the grains have already ripened, so too is the authority of the means of knowledge fruitless for those whose legal proceedings have been settled.
Even that which is untrue, if spoken at the appropriate time, is examined;

but that which is not spoken due to negligence is lost, even if it be true. Even that which is untrue, if spoken at the appropriate time, is examined; but that which is not spoken due to negligence is lost, even if it be true.

If anyone should think that a case has been decided or adjudicated contrary to the law, he shall impose double the fine and have that matter reopened. If anyone should think that a case has been decided or adjudicated contrary to the law, he shall impose double the fine and have that matter reopened.
But when a legal proceeding is wrongly judged, the members of the court shall incur that punishment; for indeed, no one ever remains on the path of righteousness without the threat of punishment.

Whoever speaks otherwise out of passion, ignorance, or greed—that member of the assembly is to be known as no true member; the king should severely punish him. Whoever speaks otherwise out of passion, ignorance, or greed—that member of the assembly is to be known as no true member; the king should severely punish him.

However, by a king who especially desires to protect his own duty, the goodness or wickedness [of others] must be examined due to the diversity of human minds. However, by a king who especially desires to protect his own duty, the goodness or wickedness [of others] must be examined due to the diversity of human minds.

There are men who, out of greed, would give false testimony; and there are other evil-minded people who forge documents. There are men who, out of greed, would give false testimony; and there are other evil-minded people who forge documents.
Therefore, both of these must be examined especially by the king:
the written document according to the rules for documents,
and the witnesses according to the rules for witnesses.
Unreal things appear like the real, and real things appear as unreal;
various entities are seen in this way. Therefore, critical investigation is appropriate.
Unreal things appear like the real, and real things appear as unreal; various entities are seen in this way. Therefore, critical investigation is appropriate.
The sky appears as if it has a surface, and a firefly like a flame;
yet no surface exists in the sky, nor is there fire in the firefly.
The sky appears as if it has a surface, and a firefly like a flame; yet no surface exists in the sky, nor is there fire in the firefly.
Therefore, it is proper to examine even an object seen through direct perception;
by making known objects after having examined them, one does not fall away from dharma.
Therefore, it is proper to examine even an object seen through direct perception; by making known objects after having examined them, one does not fall away from dharma.
Seeing [the truth] thus at all times, the king, composed in mind while attending to legal affairs,
spreads his radiant glory here and attains the realm of the Sun.
Seeing [the truth] thus at all times, the king, composed in mind while attending to legal affairs, spreads his radiant glory here and attains the realm of the Sun.

"But the plaintiff, having firmly established his strength and impelled by his own interest..."
Having firmly established his strength and being impelled by his own cause, the plaintiff, having reached a definitive conclusion regarding the matter to be accomplished,
shall have the plaint written down.

But the defendant, having heard the meaning of the plaintiff's case, should immediately thereafter present his counter-argument connected to the matter of that plaintiff's case. But the defendant, having heard the meaning of the plaintiff's case, should immediately thereafter present his counter-argument connected to the matter of that plaintiff's case.
The plaintiff may obtain the filing of the written petition after one day, or after three days, or even after seven days;

however, if he is engaged in the third quarter [of the day], he will certainly be victorious immediately. He may obtain the filing of the written petition after one day, or after three days, or even after seven days; however, if he is engaged in the third quarter [of the day], he will certainly be victorious immediately.
The reply (uttara) may be of four kinds: denial (mithyā), admission (saṃpratipatti), a counter-pleading (pratyavaskanda), or a plea based on a prior judgment (prāṅnyāyavidhisādhya). (NarS 2.4)
"This is false; I do not know it, for I was not present there at that time;
and I was not even born at that moment"—thus is falsehood fourfold.
"This is false; I do not know it, for I was not present there at that time; and I was not even born at that moment"—thus is falsehood fourfold.

The rejoinder (uttara) may be of four kinds: the false (mithyā), the contrary (viparīta), the verbal (śabdasamāgama), and that which relates to the meaning of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣārthasaṃbandha). NarS 2.6. The rejoinder may be of four kinds: the false, the contrary, the verbal, and that which relates to the meaning of the prima facie argument.
The defendant shall not submit a reply until the plaintiff has caused the plaint to be written down;
indeed, the plaintiff shall cause it to be written down for as long as the matter intended to be stated remains.

The defendant shall not submit a reply until the plaintiff has caused the plaint to be written down; indeed, the plaintiff shall cause it to be written down for as long as the matter intended to be stated remains.
A document that has a different meaning, one devoid of substance, one lacking authoritative sources or tradition,
one with omissions or additions, and one that is corrupted— these are declared to be defects of speech.

(Narada Smṛti 2.8) A document that has a different meaning, one devoid of substance, one lacking authoritative sources or tradition, one with omissions or additions, and one that is corrupted— these are declared to be defects of speech.

Whatever is to be obtained by whom, from whatever source—that person shall obtain that from that; but neither another [person] obtains it, nor does one obtain something else, nor from anything else. Thus, this threefold [formula] is for the sake of establishing the correspondence between things. Whatever is to be obtained by whom, from whatever source—that person shall obtain that from that; but neither another [person] obtains it, nor does one obtain something else, nor from anything else. Thus, this threefold [formula] is for the sake of establishing the correspondence between things.

I too have been meditated upon here by your friend with a mind like that of an enemy; therefore, it is because of his great forbearance that you have been informed of this by me. I too have been meditated upon here by your friend with a mind like that of an enemy; therefore, it is because of his great forbearance that you have been informed of this by me.
That which is deficient in the measurement of substance, devoid of the support of the result, and lacking in authority—
this defect of the document known as "devoid of authority" (pramāṇavarjita) one should reject.

(NarS 2.11) That which is deficient in the measurement of substance, devoid of the support of the result, and lacking in authority— this defect of the document known as "devoid of authority" one should reject.
In the first quarter [of the verse], one should avoid a fault that is devoid of scriptural authority;
[one should also avoid] a single person acting in opposition to many, or one who causes conflict between a city and a kingdom.

If there be a deficiency or excess in the bindu, the mātrā, the word, or the syllable—due to a single irregularity—it becomes useless; one should therefore avoid it with effort. If there be a deficiency or excess in the bindu, the mātrā, the word, or the syllable—due to a single irregularity—it becomes useless; one should therefore avoid it with effort.

One should clearly avoid even that which is corrupted or poorly situated, ruined by water, oil, and the like; in common speech, one should likewise avoid that which is clear yet has an obscure meaning. *Narasiṃhapurāṇa 2.14* One should clearly avoid even that which is corrupted or poorly situated, ruined by water, oil, and the like; in common speech, one should likewise avoid that which is clear yet has an obscure meaning. *Narasiṃhapurāṇa 2.14*

Even if a statement is well-established, it does not constitute truth if it deviates from external, established worldly conventions. Even if a statement is well-established, it does not constitute truth if it deviates from external, established worldly conventions.
That which was offered by me while residing on Gandhamādana belongs to this [deity];
it is external to the dharma of worldly transaction and is not established [as valid].
That which was offered by me while residing on Gandhamādana belongs to this [deity]; it is external to the dharma of worldly transaction and is not established [as valid].

By the insertion of different syllables and by the shifting toward a different meaning, the ritual gift becomes confused, and the ritual itself likewise becomes confused. By the insertion of different syllables and by the shifting toward a different meaning, the ritual gift becomes confused, and the ritual itself likewise becomes confused.

Whatever [the opponent] declares in the course of the procedure when provoked by one of the passions such as attachment (rāga) and so forth—all that should first be written down by the proponent on a wooden board or similar surface.

(NarS 2.18) Whatever [the opponent] declares in the course of the procedure when provoked by one of the passions such as attachment (rāga) and so forth—all that should first be written down by the proponent on a wooden board or similar surface. (NarS 2.18)
For the sake of unconfused understanding, that which has been well-examined by those established in the Dharma should be accepted;
therefore, the proponent must exclude anything else, such as the wooden board and other implements.

For the sake of unconfused understanding, that which has been well-examined by those established in the Dharma should be accepted; therefore, the proponent must exclude anything else, such as the wooden board and other implements.

With the permission of both disputants, they shall record on a wooden board the remainder of the case, along with the witnesses and the admissions of both disputants. NarS_2.20 With the permission of both disputants, they shall record on a wooden board the remainder of the case, along with the witnesses and the admissions of both disputants.

That which remains from what was written by the two disputants, and which is subsequently remembered by a disputant, is called *pratyākalita*; it is recorded by him under his own heading. NarS_m2.21 That which remains from what was written by the two disputants, and which is subsequently remembered by a disputant, is called *pratyākalita*; it is recorded by him under his own heading.

Whether appointed by the plaintiff or even sent by the defendant, whoever litigates on behalf of another, victory and defeat belong to those two [parties]. Whether appointed by the plaintiff or even sent by the defendant, whoever litigates on behalf of another, victory and defeat belong to those two [parties].

He who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor one acting under a legal mandate, yet speaks for the sake of another, shall be punished if he gives false testimony even in a judicial proceeding.

He who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor one acting under a legal mandate, yet speaks for the sake of another, shall be punished if he gives false testimony even in a judicial proceeding.

He who, having abandoned his previous position, again takes up another, should be known as a person of inferior argument because of that shifting of the debate. He who, having abandoned his previous position, again takes up another, should be known as a person of inferior argument because of that shifting of the debate.
In all disputes, one does not lose the case through verbal quibble;
however, in matters concerning cattle, women, land, and the non-payment of debts, even if punished, one loses the object of the suit.

In all disputes, one does not lose the case through verbal quibble; however, in matters concerning cattle, women, land, and the non-payment of debts, even if punished, one loses the object of the suit.

If the defendant denies the charge, the plaintiff must point out the evidence, provided he has not been "overcome" (pratyavaskandita). If the defendant denies the charge, the plaintiff must point out the evidence, provided he has not been "overcome."
For what was written in the first part, letter by letter and in its entirety,
the claimant shall establish through action in the third part.
For what was written in the first part, letter by letter and in its entirety, the claimant shall establish through action in the third part.
Action is also said to be of two kinds: human and likewise divine. Human action is known from documents and witnesses; the ordeal by balance and so forth is recorded as divine.
When a legal proceeding has been conducted during the day in villages or cities, and witnesses are available, divine means of proof (divya) are not to be employed.
In a forest, in a deserted place, at night, inside a house,
in cases of violence, and in the denial of a deposit,
divine means of proof are applicable.

When the prima facie case has been contradicted by the presentation of a reason, the defendant must indeed act with diligence; it should be understood as being like the prima facie case itself. *NarS 2.31*:
When the prima facie case has been contradicted by the presentation of a reason, the defendant must indeed act with diligence; it should be understood as being like the prima facie case itself.

One who flees when summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by the witnesses, and one who confesses of his own accord— these are the four types of defeated litigants. 2.32 One who flees when summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by the witnesses, and one who confesses of his own accord— these are the four types of defeated litigants.
One who speaks otherwise, one who hates the performance of the rite, one who does not appear, one who is without an answer, and one who flees when summoned— these five are recorded as defeated.

Gems such as rubies, gold coins such as dīnāras, pearls, coral, conch shells, and the like, if they are stolen, go to the owner once they have been restored. || NarS_2.34 || Gems such as rubies, gold coins such as dīnāras, pearls, coral, conch shells, and the like, if they are stolen, go to the owner once they have been restored. || NarS_2.34 ||

But if one steps upon perfume, a garland, an ornament, a garment, or even a sandal— whether given or not given— the king has declared that such a person deserves death. (NarS 2.35) But if one steps upon perfume, a garland, an ornament, a garment, or even a sandal— whether given or not given— the king has declared that such a person deserves death.
The price of goods,

wages, deposits, fines, and whatever is subject to legal dispute; as well as gifts made in vain, stakes in gambling, and wagers— these do not increase [with interest] unless they are intended to do so.

Those of Śūdra birth who bring false accusations against the twice-born— the king shall have their tongues cut out and impaled upon a stake. *NarS_m2.37* Those of Śūdra birth who bring false accusations against the twice-born— the king shall have their tongues cut out and impaled upon a stake.

Whether it be a royal edict, a letter, a formal decree, a charter, a mortgage deed, a sale, or a purchase—whosoever first makes a formal representation to the king, he is to be recognized as the plaintiff by those who know the law. (Ajñā, lekha, paṭṭaka, or śāsana; whether it be a pledge, a document, a sale, or a purchase—whosoever first makes a representation to the king, he is to be known as the plaintiff by those learned in the rules.)
When witnesses are challenged, the prior purification of those witnesses must be carried out;
once the witnesses have been proven pure, one should thereafter purify the testimony itself.
When witnesses are challenged, the prior purification of those witnesses must be carried out; once the witnesses have been proven pure, one should thereafter purify the testimony itself.

If witnesses or members of the court are dismissed, there is a rule for their re-examination; however, for those who have been dismissed due to their own misconduct, there is no provision for a second trial.
Even if he has confessed by himself, or even if he has been restrained by his own conduct,

or even if he has failed in his ritual duties, he deserves the final determination by the assembly. Even if he has confessed by himself, or even if he has been restrained by his own conduct, or even if he has failed in his ritual duties, he deserves the final determination by the assembly.

The members of the court should determine the case only after setting aside the arguments; if a decision is made without setting them aside, there will be contradiction both in this world and after death.

If he is defeated by the assessors themselves, he shall afterwards be punished by the king according to his own legal code; and the document of victory (jayapatraka) should also be duly granted to the victor.
This gateway to legal procedure was previously declared by the Self-Existent One;
for when the gateway is pure, the legal procedure shall be pure, and not otherwise.
This gateway to legal procedure was previously declared by the Self-Existent One; for when the gateway is pure, the legal procedure shall be pure, and not otherwise.
3. However, one appointed to the assembly must speak words free from partiality. One appointed [to the assembly] must speak words free from partiality.
A member of the assembly who speaks what is appropriate shall incur neither hatred nor guilt; but a member of the assembly who speaks otherwise shall incur both of those.

The king, however, should appoint righteous and well-tested councilors who are capable of bearing the burden of legal proceedings, like excellent oxen. The king, however, should appoint righteous and well-tested councilors who are capable of bearing the burden of legal proceedings, like excellent oxen.
The members of the king's court should be well-versed in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras, of noble birth, speakers of truth, and impartial toward both enemy and friend.
Dharma is known to be established upon that [the king], and the king is the root of Dharma; therefore,
the king should purify legal proceedings in the company of the virtuous.
When legal proceedings are pure, the members of the court attain purity;

for their purity comes from *dharma*, therefore one should speak only what is *dharma*. When legal proceedings are pure, the members of the court attain purity; for their purity comes from *dharma*, therefore one should speak only what is *dharma*.

Where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood, while the members look on, there the members of the assembly are themselves slain. Where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood, while the members look on, there the members of the assembly are themselves slain.
